newsitem.title: USA: Iridium IPO features satellite network.
newsitem.headline: Iridium IPO features satellite network.

text.p: Investors will be offered stock sometime next week in a developing global satellite network that would link wireless telephones from the Aleutians to Zanzibar.
A 10 million share initial public offering of Iridium World Communications Ltd is expected to be launched at an estimated price of $19 to $21 a share.

"There is a general realization that there is a need for a global satellite network expanding beyond cellular phones," said Mona Eraiba, technology analyst at Gruntal & Co. "My sense is it (the offering) will be successful."
Iridium World represents about an eight percent stake in Iridium LLC, a consortium including Motorola Inc, Sprint Corp, Lockheed Martin Corp and Raytheon Co.

It plans to operate a global telephone service via 66 low-orbit satellites, a network estimated to cost $3.4 billion that would allow wireless phone calls to and from anywhere in the world. Cellular phone and communications services are now limited to specific service areas.
Proceeds from the offer will be used to pay for development costs and other general corporate purposes.

"There are a lot of signs this kind of satellite (network) is going to be very valuable," Eraiba said, adding that, depending on market conditions, the share price could rise to $23 to $24 on the first day of trade.
Iridium spokesman John Windolph declined to comment on the offering.

Iridium had planned to launch its first five satellites in January, but technical problems and an unrelated explosion of a McDonnell Douglas Corp Delta II rocket, the type also used to launch Iridium satellites, delayed the launch until May.
Windolph said the company has scheduled its next launch for mid-June, when seven satellites will be sent into orbit on a Proton rocket owned by a Russian rocket maker Khrunichev.
Windolph said that, despite various launch delays, the company is on track to roll out commercial service in September of 1998. He said there will be a six-month test period prior to the rollout.
Though Iridium will likely be the first, other companies are close behind in developing satellite telecom systems.

Globalstar Telecommunications Ltd is an estimated $2.5 billion satellite phone system founded by Loral Space & Communications Ltd and Qualcomm Inc. Alcatel Espace, a unit of Alcatel Alsthom, also has a stake in Globalstar. That system is expected to be in service on January 1, 1999.
Globalstar, however, is said to be focusing on providing service to rural, hard-to-reach customers, whereas Iridium is targeting the international business user.
Analysts said competition is not an issue that would hurt the IPO.
"All the satellite services have the advantage of fixed costs and high-incremental profitability. But they're all risky," said Cai von Rumohr, managing director at Cowen & Co.
